Forecasting the House

This chapter builds a forecast of the 2026 House and Senate elections and then takes it apart. Everything in it is computed from files this book already holds, except one number, which is a guess. That number turns out to move the answer more than any of the data does.

The model is deliberately simple. It is close in shape to the professional forecasts you will read about in November, and simple enough that you can see every assumption it makes.

Both chambers are run in one simulation rather than two. That is not a convenience. It is the only way to answer “will one party hold both”, and the last third of the chapter is about why.

Why build one at all

A forecast is the only thing in political commentary that can be wrong.

That is the case for it, and it is stronger than it sounds. Say “Republicans are in trouble” and no result can contradict you. Say “the Democrats have a 90% chance of winning the House and will most likely win 244 seats” and you have written down something the world can refute. The discipline is not in the arithmetic. It is in being made to say how sure you are.

There are three more reasons, and they matter more for this course than the prediction does.

A model prices its own assumptions. You cannot build one without deciding what a district’s starting point is, what a poll measures, and how much things move. Each of those decisions is invisible in prose and unavoidable in code. By the end of this chapter you will know which of them the answer actually depends on, because you will have turned each one and watched.

A model says where the election is. This one will tell you that 67 of 435 districts are close enough to matter and 368 are not, and it will name the seat that decides the chamber. That is a claim about what to pay attention to, and you get it for free on the way to the forecast.

A model separates what is known from what is not. The polls in this chapter are measured to within half a point. The seat count that follows from them has a range of 57 seats. Both of those facts come out of the same model, and holding them together is the whole skill.

There is a case against, and it is not silly. A probability gets retold as a prediction, and an 85% chance that is retold as a certainty makes the model look broken when the 15% happens. Forecasts may change behaviour, which is a problem if you think turnout should not depend on a number. And a model built on the past cannot see anything genuinely new. None of that is an argument for predicting nothing. It is an argument for reading the interval rather than the headline, which is what the rest of this chapter is training.

What is actually being claimed

A forecast makes a claim about a distribution, not about an outcome.

“The Democrats will win 244 seats” is not what this model says, and no model says it. What it says is narrower. Given the polls, given the map, and given stated assumptions about how wrong each can be, here is a spread of outcomes and how often each one turned up. The single number in the headline is the middle of that spread, and it is the least interesting thing the model produced.

This matters because of how such a claim can be graded. One election is one draw. A model that said 85% and lost was not necessarily wrong, and a model that said 85% and won was not necessarily right. Grading a probability takes many forecasts, and this book has a chapter on exactly that problem.

The input: six aggregators, one number

The model takes one number from the outside world: how the country says it will vote for Congress. That question is asked in polls under the name the generic ballot — a survey question that asks which party’s candidate you would support in your district, without naming anybody.

No agency publishes an average of those polls. Six private outfits do, each with its own list of polls and its own corrections, and none of them publishes a file anybody else can read. What exists is a table on a Wikipedia page that puts the six side by side, which is the only reason this chapter can compare them at all.

Aggregator Democrats Republicans Other or undecided Two-party Democratic share
RealClearPolitics 48.6 41.6 9.8 53.88
Race to the WH 47.8 40.9 11.3 53.89
Decision Desk HQ 46.9 40.1 13.0 53.91
VoteHub 48.6 41.9 9.5 53.70
Silver Bulletin 48.3 41.7 9.8 53.67
FiftyPlusOne 49.2 42.7 8.1 53.54

The six agree to within 0.5 points. Read down the last column and they are as close as measurements of the same thing ever get. That is worth pausing on, because it is the last time in this chapter that anything will be this well determined.

The last column is the one the model uses, and it is not the headline margin. Between a tenth and an eighth of respondents pick neither party, and the share of them differs across the six by 4.9 points. Dropping those respondents and recomputing each party’s share of the rest gives the two-party share, which is the unit district returns come in. The average lands at 53.73% Democratic, or D+7.5 on the margin.

Six aggregators reading the same polls in the same week. The spread between them is 0.5 points. Hover for each aggregator's full numbers.

Figure 1. Six aggregators, one week, one question. Each dot is one organisation’s average of the same public polls. The dotted line is the average of the six, +6.7. Their disagreement is 0.5 points, which is smaller than the width of the dots on most screens.

The baseline: 435 districts, and the 38 with one name on the ballot

A national number cannot elect anybody. Seats are won district by district, so the model needs a starting share for each of the 435.

The obvious starting share is what happened last time: the Democratic share of the two-party vote in that district in 2024, from the Clerk of the House’s official returns. That works for 397 districts and fails for 38 of them, because those races had only one major-party candidate. There is no Democratic share of a two-party vote when there was no two-party vote.

Those 38 seats cannot be dropped. A forecast that ignores 9% of the House is not a forecast of the House. So each of them is given a starting share predicted from something that does exist everywhere: the presidential vote inside that district in 2024.

Quantity Value
Districts with a two-party House result 397
Districts without one 38
How closely the presidential vote tracks the House vote r-squared 0.974
Typical miss when it is used to predict the House vote 2.5 points

The presidential vote inside a district now predicts its House vote almost exactly. Across the 397 districts that had two candidates, the relationship is tight enough that the typical miss is 2.5 points. That is a fact about this decade and not about House elections in general, and the next section shows how recently it became true.

Two seats the official returns do not number

Two districts arrive with no vote total for either party.

District Democratic share of the 2024 presidential vote Assigned to
FL-20 69.70 D
OK-03 26.53 R

The Clerk prints a footnote marker where the vote count goes when a candidate ran unopposed in certain states, and the reader is meant to understand that the one name on the page won. A program reads two zeros and concludes that neither party won the seat.

So the winner cannot be read off the arithmetic, and both seats are assigned here to the party that carried the district’s presidential vote. That is a rule and not a lookup, and it would be wrong in a district that split its ticket. Neither of these is within twenty points of the line, which is why it is safe here and would not be somewhere else. It is stated because a reader who does not know it would think the House had 433 members.

Quantity Value
Democratic seats the baseline produces 215
Democratic seats in the 2024 House 215
Seats within 5 points of the line 67
Seats more than 5 points from it 368

67 seats start within five points of the line. The other 368 decide nothing. Whatever happens in November, more than four out of five districts already know their answer, and a national swing of any plausible size will not reach them. That is the first thing this model tells you, and it is not a prediction.

The model, in three lines

Here is the whole thing.

  1. Swing. Take the national two-party vote you are assuming, and subtract what it actually was in 2024. The polls imply 53.73% minus 48.65%, which is +5.08 points.
  2. Shift. Add that swing to every district’s starting share. Add two random errors: one drawn once and applied to all 435 seats, one drawn separately for each seat.
  3. Count. Every district above 50 is a Democratic seat. Do it 20,000 times.

The two errors are the interesting part, and the difference between them is the whole reason a forecast has a probability on it at all.

The national error is one number applied to every district. It stands for the things that move the country together: the polls being off, the last three months not going as expected, an electorate that turns out differently from the one the pollsters modeled. If it is +2, every district is two points more Democratic than the baseline said.

The district error is drawn fresh for each seat. It stands for a retirement, a scandal, a candidate who cannot raise money, a local issue. These are real and they are independent, and 435 independent errors mostly cancel.

That word mostly is doing a great deal of work, and the section after next is about how much.

What the map does to the vote

Before any error is added, the model is a plain function: give it a national vote share, get back a seat count. That function is the map.

Seats the model gives the Democrats at each national vote share, with no error term switched on. The step at each district is one seat changing hands. Hover anywhere on the plot.

Figure 2. Seats against votes on the 2024 map. The vertical axis is Democratic seats and the horizontal axis is the national two-party Democratic share of the House vote. The dashed line at 218 is a majority.

Two readings come off it.

The Democrats reach 218 seats at 49.2% of the national vote, which is a margin of R+1.6. They can lose the national House vote by 1.6 points and still hold the chamber. The seat that delivers the majority is PA-07, the 218th district counting down from the most Democratic, which starts at 49.5%.

The curve runs at about 4.52 seats per point of national vote. That is the exchange rate between a poll and a chamber, and it is what makes the rest of the chapter arithmetic rather than argument. An error of two points in the polling average is an error of roughly 9 seats in the answer.

Before you read on, write two numbers down. The polls imply a national Democratic share of 53.73%, and the curve above says that is worth 237 seats. Now add the uncertainty back. How wide is the 80% interval around that seat count — that is, how many seats separate the 10th percentile from the 90th? And what probability would you put on the Democrats winning the House? Commit to both before you look.

The forecast, with the dials exposed

The distribution of Democratic seats over 20,000 simulated elections. Move any dial. Everything below it recomputes.

Figure 3. 20,000 simulated elections. Each bar is a seat count and its height is how often that count came up. Bars at or above 218 are a Democratic House. At the polling average the model gives the Democrats a median of 244 seats, an 80% interval of 218 to 275, and a 90% chance of a majority.

Move the first slider and you are asking a different question of the same model. Move the second and third and you are changing what the model believes about its own reliability, without touching a single piece of data.

Three things are worth doing before you read on.

Set the environment to a tied national vote. The median falls to about 219 seats and the chance of a Democratic House to roughly even. That is the tipping point from Figure 2 arriving as a probability. This one slider is what decides the answer.

Set the district error to zero. The median does not move. It lands on 237 seats, which is exactly the point Figure 2 gave with no simulation at all. Independent district errors change the width and not the centre.

Set the assumed polling error to zero, then drag it as far right as it goes. The interval more than doubles in width, and the probability falls by about fifteen points rather than collapsing. That is not what most readers expect, and the reason is worth holding on to. When the central estimate sits 26 seats past the threshold, making the interval symmetrically wider adds outcomes on both sides. It takes a great deal of extra doubt to move a probability that is not already near a coin flip.

Which is the honest verdict on that dial. The assumed polling error is the least defensible number in this chapter, and it changes the headline seat range a great deal and the headline probability rather less. Both of those are worth knowing, and only one of them makes the news.

Where the uncertainty comes from

The two error terms are not equal partners, and the gap between them is the single most useful thing in this chapter.

Error terms switched on 10th percentile 90th percentile Width, seats Chance of a Democratic House
national error only 222 266 44 94%
district error only 239 250 11 100%
both 218 275 57 90%

Turn off the district error and the interval barely narrows: from 57 seats to 44. Turn off the national error instead and it collapses to 11. Nearly all of the uncertainty in a 435-seat forecast comes from one number drawn once.

The reason is arithmetic rather than politics. The district error is drawn independently 435 times, and independent errors cancel: some seats break one way, some the other, and the total moves very little. The national error does not cancel, because there is only one of it. When the polls are two points off, they are two points off everywhere at once.

The same 80% interval, with one error term switched on at a time. Hover a bar.

Figure 4. The same forecast with one error term at a time. The dot is the median in all three cases; only the width changes. The district error is 4.5 points per seat and buys 11 seats of range. The national error is 3.0 points, once, and buys 44.

This is why professional forecasts do not report 99% very often, and why adding more district-level detail to a model does less than it looks like it should. Better candidate data shrinks the small term. Nothing shrinks the large one except better polls.

Does it work?

The model can be run on elections that already happened, which is the only way to find out.

The test is deliberately generous. Take two consecutive elections on unchanged district lines, hand the model the second election’s actual national vote, and ask it only for the seat count. It is being told the answer to the hard part.

From To Districts National swing Model said Actually Model missed by No-change missed by
2004 2006 316 5.30 158 168 -10 -22
2006 2008 316 1.70 179 188 -9 -20
2008 2010 316 -9.19 147 138 9 45
2012 2014 326 -3.68 128 132 -4 13
2014 2016 408 2.41 186 183 3 -5
2016 2018 408 5.00 198 222 -24 -38
2018 2020 435 -2.86 211 222 -11 13
2022 2024 435 0.10 213 215 -2 -3

The model missed by 9 seats on average. Assuming nothing changed at all missed by 19.9. So the machinery earns its keep, and by less than you might expect for something with 435 moving parts.

Two failures are visible in that table and neither is noise.

It understates waves. Sort the eight pairs by how far the country moved and the errors line up against them: the correlation between the national swing and the model’s error is -0.66. The two ends make it plain. 2006 and 2018 are the two largest Democratic swings here, and the model gave the Democrats 10 and 24 seats too few. 2010 is the largest Republican swing, and it erred 9 the other way. When the country moves hard, competitive districts move harder than safe ones, and a model that shifts every district equally cannot represent that.

Its errors are correlated within a year, which is the same fact as the previous section from a different direction. The misses are not scattered around zero district by district. They are whole elections coming out wrong together.

That is where the model’s own uncertainty comes from. The spread of those 8 errors, divided by the 4.52 seats each point of national vote is worth, is 2.21 points of vote. That number is measured, and it is added to the polling-error guess to make the national error the simulation uses.

Eight pairs of consecutive elections on unchanged district lines. The model was told the national vote and asked only for the seats. Hover a year.

Figure 5. The model against eight elections it was allowed to see the answer to. Each point is one election, placed by what actually happened and what the model said. Points on the diagonal are exact. Points below it gave the Democrats too few seats.

Four other answers to the same question

The model above is one way to answer “who will hold the House”. Here are four more, in order of how much data each one needs.

Model What it uses Democratic seats 80% interval Chance of a Democratic House
No change Nothing. Last election repeats. 215 — —
The midterm penalty One sentence and 41 past midterms. 243 211 to 287 88%
Uniform swing The polling average and the 2024 map. 237 — —
Uniform swing, simulated The same, plus a national and a district error term. 244 218 to 275 90%
FiftyPlusOne Polls, fundraising, past returns, candidate data and race ratings, House and Senate together. 230 211 to 253 85%

Every model here that states a probability lands between 85% and 90%. The one-sentence base rate from the midterm-penalty chapter is the president’s party loses House seats. It and a professional model built on polls, fundraising, candidate files and race ratings differ by 5 points of probability.

What the data buys is not a different answer. It is a narrower one. The base rate’s interval is 76 seats wide; the professional model’s is 42. That is the return on all of it, and it is real without being dramatic.

This model sits 14 seats more Democratic than the professional one and calls a wider interval. Both gaps have an explanation and neither is flattering. The extra optimism is mostly incumbency. This model has no idea which seats have a retiring member, and the seats around the line are held disproportionately by Democrats who ran ahead of their district in 2024. The extra width is the model admitting it has fewer inputs.

Five answers to one question, with the interval each one states. Hover for what each model uses.

Figure 6. Five models, one axis. The dot is each model’s central estimate and the bar is its 80% interval where it states one. The percentages on the right are each model’s chance of a Democratic House.

The other chamber

The Senate is on the same ballot, and it is a different problem.

Only a third of it faces the voters at a time. 33 seats are up in 2026 — the Class 2 seats, which is a fact about the calendar and not a forecast. The other 67 are not up, and their holders are already known.

Quantity Value
Seats up in 2026 33
… held by Democrats going in 13
Seats not up, held by Democrats or independents who caucus with them 34
Seats not up, held by Republicans 33
Seats a Democratic majority needs 51
… so seats they must win of the ones up 17
… which is a net gain of 4

Two things in that table are decisions rather than counts, and both change the answer. The two independents caucus with the Democrats, so they are counted on that side; no party column in any file records this. And a Democratic majority needs 51, not 50, because the Vice President breaks ties and will be a Republican until January 2029. Move either and the target moves with it.

The baseline is worse here, and it has to be

A House district’s starting share was what that district did in 2024, because the whole House ran in 2024. These Senate seats last ran in 2020, six years and two very different elections ago. So the starting share is the state’s 2024 presidential vote instead.

That has a consequence worth stating plainly. The Senate model does not reproduce the Senate. At a swing of zero it hands the Democrats the 12 states Harris carried, and the Democrats actually hold 13 of these seats. The House model hid this problem by starting from a real House result. The Senate model cannot, so the incumbency the House model quietly inherited is missing here in full view.

How far a Senate race runs from its state

The state-level error is measured the same way as the House’s, on 112 past races across 4 elections.

Election Kind Races measured Points from the state’s presidential vote, sd
2014 midterm 30 6.02
2018 midterm 29 8.12
2020 presidential year 25 3.67
2022 midterm 28 3.46

A Senate race lands 6.1 points from its state’s presidential vote at a midterm. A House district lands 4.0 points from its own. Senate candidates matter more than House candidates, which is the expected answer and is worth having as a number rather than as a belief.

The by-year column is the honest caveat. It runs from 3.5 to 8.1 and it has been falling, so 6.1 averages two elections in which candidates mattered a great deal with a recent one in which they mattered much less. A smaller figure would be defensible and would make the Senate look more predictable than it does here.

The cliff

All 33 seats up in 2026, ordered by how their state voted for president in 2024. Democrats need the top 17. Hover a seat.

Figure 7. The 33 seats, in order. Each dot is one seat up in 2026, placed by the Democratic share of its state’s 2024 presidential vote and coloured by which party holds it now. The dashed line is the 17th seat.

Democrats reach 51 seats at 54.4% of the national vote — a margin of D+8.8. The House needs 49.2%, a margin of R+1.6. The same election, the same national swing, and the two chambers are 10.4 points of margin apart in what they demand.

The figure shows why. Below Maine and North Carolina there is a gap of about 5.1 points before the next Republican seat. Democrats can win the two obvious targets and still be short, and the seats after that are six or seven points further away. The House has a tipping point; the Senate has a cliff.

Both chambers, one election

Now the question that needed the Senate.

Outcome One national error, shared A separate error for each chamber
Democratic House 90% 90%
Democratic Senate 59% 59%
Both chambers 59% 53%
Neither chamber 9% 4%
One of the two 32% 43%

Both chambers is 59% when the two share a national error and 53% when they do not. Treating them as independent means multiplying the two chambers’ probabilities together, which gives 53%. The right answer is 5 points higher.

The reason is the same national error the House section was about. A polling miss is not a House event. If the polls are two points too Republican, they are two points too Republican in Georgia and Maine as well as in Pennsylvania’s 7th. Good years are good in both chambers and bad years are bad in both, so the two outcomes arrive together far more often than independence would allow.

Every simulated election placed by both of its outcomes, binned four House seats wide. Switch the error structure with the buttons.

Figure 8. Every simulated election, placed by both of its outcomes. The horizontal axis is Democratic House seats and the vertical axis Democratic Senate seats. The dashed lines are the two majorities, and the shaded corner is a Democratic sweep.

Switch the buttons and watch the cloud change shape. With one shared national error the two chambers correlate at 0.82 and the cloud leans. Give each chamber its own error and the correlation falls to about zero and the cloud goes round. Both pictures use the same seats, the same polls and the same district data. The only difference is whether one draw is shared or two are drawn.

Against the model this chapter is copying

Quantity FiftyPlusOne This model FiftyPlusOne, if the chambers were independent
House 85% 90% —
Senate 55% 59% —
Both chambers 53% 59% 47%

Both forecasts show the same effect at almost the same size. FiftyPlusOne publishes 85% for the House and 55% for the Senate, which multiply to 47% — and they publish 53% for both. This model’s gap is 5 points and theirs is 6. Two independently built models agreeing on the size of a correction is about as much corroboration as this chapter can offer for anything.

One structural result is worth saying out loud. A Democratic Senate without a Democratic House happens in 0.2% of simulations. The Senate is the harder chamber by seven points of national margin, so essentially every environment good enough to deliver it has already delivered the House. The interesting uncertainty is not which chamber, it is whether the year is good enough for the second one.

What this model cannot tell you

The map it is built on will not be used

Every district in the baseline is a 2024 district, and 10 states have enacted new congressional maps since.

State Democratic-leaning seats Highly competitive seats Republican-leaning seats
California 4 -3 -1
Utah 1 0 -1
Alabama 0 -1 1
North Carolina 0 -1 1
Florida 1 -4 3
Louisiana -1 0 1
Ohio 0 -2 2
Tennessee -1 0 1
Missouri -1 -1 2
Texas -3 -2 5

The redraws removed 14 competitive seats and produced a net +14 Republican-leaning ones. The partisan effect roughly cancels: Texas, Florida, Missouri, Ohio and North Carolina drew seats toward the Republicans, California and Utah toward the Democrats, and the net across the Democratic column is +0.

The effect on the model does not cancel. This model’s uncertainty lives entirely in competitive districts, and the map has 14 fewer of them than the one the forecast is built on. A more careful version would rebuild every changed district’s baseline from precinct returns, which is a real piece of work and not a correction.

It does not know who is running

38 seats had one major-party candidate in 2024 and were given a starting share by prediction. Every seat’s starting share carries the incumbent who won it, and incumbents retire. Something over fifty members have announced they will not seek re-election, and each of those seats reverts toward its underlying partisanship in a way this model has no way to see.

That is not a small omission. It is most of the difference between this model and a professional one, and it points the same direction every time: an open seat is worth less to the party that held it.

One election cannot grade a probability

The forecast says 90%. In November one thing will happen. No single outcome can show that number was right or wrong, and the temptation to treat the result as a verdict on the model is very strong and completely unfounded. Grading probabilistic forecasts takes many of them, scored a particular way, and that is a separate problem this book takes up elsewhere.

One of its inputs is a judgment, not a measurement

The national error is 3.0 points of two-party share. Of that, 2.21 was measured from the backtest and 2.00 was assumed. Here is what turning the assumed part does.

Assumed polling error Median Democratic seats 80% interval Width Chance of a Democratic House
±0.0 points of margin 244 224 to 267 43 seats 96%
±1.0 points of margin 244 224 to 267 43 seats 95%
±2.0 points of margin 244 222 to 269 47 seats 94%
±3.0 points of margin 244 220 to 272 52 seats 92%
±4.0 points of margin 245 218 to 275 57 seats 90%

Turning that dial from zero to the default widens the interval by 14 seats and moves the probability by 5 points. So the guess matters much more to the range than to the headline. Both numbers get published and only the headline gets repeated, which is the reverse of where the guess actually lands.

That is not a defence of the guess. Everything else in this chapter is computed from a file somebody published. This one is a judgment, it cannot be checked inside the model, and there is no version of this exercise in which it goes away.

The Senate half is the weaker half

Three things make it so, and none of them has a cheap fix.

Its baseline is a presidential result, so it carries no incumbency at all. The House model started from an actual House election and inherited every incumbent’s personal vote for free. These seats last ran in 2020, so the Senate model starts from how the state voted for president and knows nothing about the person on the ballot. Maine is the standing example: the model treats it as a Harris state at 53.5% and has no way to represent a Republican who has survived it five times.

Thirty-three is a small number. The House’s district errors cancel across 435 seats. Across 33 they cancel much less, so the Senate distribution is wider relative to its threshold, and one or two races carry real weight.

The state error is unstable. It has run from 3.5 to 8.1 points across the four elections measured, and it has been falling. This model uses 6.1, the midterm average. A reader who thought 2022 was the better guide would use about half that and would get a noticeably different Senate probability from the same data.

What a hundred lines of arithmetic can testify to

The evidence behind this forecast is four things. The Clerk of the House’s official district returns for 2024. The presidential vote inside each of those districts and in each state. A roster saying which Senate seats face the voters and who holds the rest. And one polling average that six organisations agree on to within 0.5 points. Everything else is arithmetic performed in the open.

What it establishes is narrower than a seat count. The 2024 map gives the Democrats a House majority at 49.2% of the national two-party vote, so they can lose that vote by 1.6 points and still hold the chamber. The Senate does not arrive until 54.4%. 67 districts are close enough to matter. The exchange rate is about 4.52 seats per point. Those facts are about the map, they do not depend on any poll, and they would be worth knowing if nobody ever ran a simulation.

The joint result is the one that could not be got any other way. Both chambers comes out at 59%, against 53% if the two were treated as independent events. That 5-point difference is not a refinement. It is the whole content of the claim that a polling miss happens to a country rather than to a chamber.

What it cannot establish is which of 218 to 275 seats will happen. That range is not a failure of effort. It is 3.0 points of national uncertainty multiplied by 4.52 seats per point, and the only way to narrow it is to know the national vote better than anybody currently does.

The uncomfortable version is the one the model comparison gives. One sentence you can say out loud, the president’s party loses House seats, got within 3 points of probability of a professional forecast built on polls, money, candidates and expert ratings. All of the data narrowed the interval. None of it changed the answer.

These are used only to measure how far a Senate race lands from its state’s presidential vote. 112 of 129 races carried a two-party share for both parties; the rest had a major party missing, a jungle primary or a runoff, and were refused rather than guessed at.
  • Wikipedia, “2026 United States House of Representatives elections” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections), fetched as wikitext, for two tables: the comparison of six generic-ballot aggregators, and the state-by-state summary of mid-decade redistricting. Wikipedia is not the authority on either. It is used because the six aggregators — Decision Desk HQ, FiftyPlusOne, RealClearPolitics, Silver Bulletin, VoteHub and Race to the WH — publish no common file, and this is the only place they appear side by side.
  • FiftyPlusOne, “Election forecast: Democrats strongly favored for the House, tilt Senate” (3 August 2026), https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/election-forecast-democrats-strongly-favored-house-tilt-senate, for the professional forecast this chapter is modeled on and compared against. Its published figures are quoted, not recomputed.

The one number that is not from a file

  • The assumed polling error, 2.00 points of two-party share (4.0 points of margin). Published assessments of final generic-ballot averages put the typical miss in that neighbourhood, with 2022 larger. The average used here is three months before the election rather than final, which is a further reason not to set it lower.

The data itself

Every figure above is drawn from these tables. They are plain CSV, they open in a spreadsheet, and they are yours to take further.

baseline.csv, calibration.csv, curve.csv, generic_ballot.csv, joint.csv, joint_cloud.csv, joint_compare.csv, models.csv, redistricting.csv, senate_calibration.csv, senate_curve.csv, senate_parse.csv, senate_sd_by_year.csv, senate_seats.csv, senate_sim.csv, sensitivity.csv, sim_default.csv, simulation.csv, spread.csv

Your turn

None of these is answered above, and every one can be answered from the tables you just opened.

  • generic_ballot.csv holds six aggregators’ numbers for the same thing. Look at the spread. Which one would you feed the model, and what does the disagreement cost you?
  • calibration.csv tests the model against past elections, with err and nochange_err beside each other. Is the model beating the assumption that nothing changes?
  • sensitivity.csv varies the assumed polling error and reports what happens to the interval. Find where the answer stops being confident. Which assumption is doing the most work?
  • baseline.csv flags districts as imputed or uncontested. Count them. How many of the districts in a national forecast are guesses rather than measurements?

  • Bafumi, J., Erikson, R. S. and Wlezien, C. (2010). “Balancing, Generic Polls and Midterm Congressional Elections.” Journal of Politics 72(3): 705–719.

Rebuild this data yourself, with an AI assistant 
I want to rebuild a public dataset from its original sources, without
any starting files. Please do the following and show your work — and
know one thing going in: part of this source moves every day, so your
copy will be today's page, not the one this book captured.

THE FIRST SOURCE. Wikipedia's page "2026 United States House of
Representatives elections", fetched as raw wikitext through the
MediaWiki API:
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections&prop=wikitext&format=json&formatversion=2
No account or key is needed. Two tables inside it matter: the
comparison of generic-ballot polling aggregators, and the summary of
mid-decade redistricting. Wikipedia is not the authority on either —
it is merely the one place six aggregators who publish no common file
sit in a single table.

THE SECOND SOURCE. The @unitedstates project's roster of sitting
members of Congress:
https://unitedstates.github.io/congress-legislators/legislators-current.csv
One CSV; each row is a current senator or representative, with party,
state and Senate class. No key.

WHAT TO BUILD.
1. The aggregators' national House margins, read out of the wikitext
   table, with their average.
2. From the roster: the Senate seats up in November 2026 — class 2,
   plus any special elections — with each seat's current party.
3. A sanity baseline: the 2024 House result the forecast starts from,
   215 Democratic seats to 220 Republican, with every district given a
   starting vote share.

CHECK YOUR WORK. The copy this book used was captured on 16 August
2026. The aggregator table will have moved since — that drift is the
page being edited, not an error. What should still hold:
- the baseline reproduces the 2024 House: 215 Democratic seats
- all 435 districts carry a starting share
- 537 rows in the roster file, and its senators sum to exactly 100
The roster updates whenever a seat changes hands mid-term; a count a
few rows off means a vacancy or a swearing-in, not a mistake.
